_doc.purpose: How held living stock changes each year (sim/world/stock_dynamics.py, sim/engine/living_stock_yearly.py). A material listed here is multiplied by its natural increase when the holding is at least its breeding minimum, and lowered by its annual loss; both are fractions of the holding, applied as expected values (no dice).
_doc.fields: walks: true for animals that are driven to market on foot (the drove mode); other stock (seed, cuttings, eggs) is carried as goods. natural_increase: fraction of the holding added in a year by breeding or propagation. annual_loss: fraction lost in a year to death, spoilage or failed sets. breeding_minimum_units: smallest holding that can breed (a breeding group, a viable planting), in the material's unit; below it nothing is added. basis: how the rates were reached. source: author or body, title and year of what the figures came from. confidence: A, B or C, the grade of that source (A a handbook or measured, C a web summary or estimate). grows_on: what limits the holding's yearly gain: pasture (the grass of the stock's place, sim/geography/food_pasture.py, and the live weight already grazing there) or arable (the arable land of the place at the output per hectare of the stock's production entry); absent means unlimited. species: the herd animal ids (data/world/geography/resources/animals.json) the stock is kept from; the held lot also loses the endemic disease loss of its place for the hardiest of them (data/disease/endemic/), and a lot whose loss outruns its natural increase dies out. The labour of any gain is the labour of that production entry, bought at the going wage; a purse that cannot pay buys less gain.
_doc.status: Every rate here is a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC unless the row carries a source: a stated order-of-magnitude estimate from the reasoning in its basis. The gain of a row with grows_on is limited by the pasture or arable land of the place and paid in labour; a row without it is not.

draught_animal_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, live weight of working cattle and horses. About half a herd is breeding females and a female calves or foals in about six years in ten, so 0.3 young per head per year; about a third of the young die or are culled before work age, leaving about 0.2. Adult mortality of a few percent a year (disease, accident, murrain) is taken as 0.05. A breeding group is a male and three females, about four animals of about 300 kg live weight, so 1200 kg. Estimates, not checked against a source.

ramie_stock_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, rhizome cuttings. Ramie spreads by rhizome and is propagated by dividing it; a stand can be divided into several times its planting weight in a year, but cuttings are held as stock here and not planted out, so only a modest 0.3 is taken for the part divided and replanted in a nursery. Rot and failed sets lose about a tenth of stored cuttings a year. A viable nursery is taken as a few kilograms of cuttings. Estimates, not checked against a source.

silkworm_eggs_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, eggs of the silkworm. A held lot does not multiply: eggs become more eggs only by being hatched, reared on mulberry leaf to cocoons and the moths allowed to lay, which is the production entry silkworm_eggs_kg, not a rate of the lot. Eggs are stored cool and hatch the following spring; a lot kept past one season loses most of its viability, so half of a held lot is taken as lost in a year. Estimates, not checked against a source.

cashmere_goat_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, live weight of fine-undercoat goats. Does kid about once a year with some twins, about one kid per doe and about half the flock are does, so 0.5 kids per head; about a third of kids die before their first winter, leaving about 0.3. Adult mortality is taken as 0.08. A breeding flock is a buck and four does, about five animals of about 30 kg, so 150 kg. Estimates, not checked against a source.

angora_goat_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, live weight of Angora goats. The same reasoning and numbers as cashmere_goat_kg: about one kid per doe, half the flock does, a third of kids lost, adult mortality 0.08, a breeding flock of five animals of about 30 kg. Estimates, not checked against a source.

jute_seed_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, jute seed. Seed multiplies only by being sown and harvested, which is the production entry jute_seed_kg, not a rate of held seed. Stored seed loses viability to damp, insects and age; about three tenths of a held lot is taken as unusable after a year. Estimates, not checked against a source.

hop_rhizome_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, hop rhizome cuttings. The hop is a perennial that is propagated by cuttings from the rootstock; a nursery of cuttings multiplies by about a third a year when divided and replanted. About a tenth of held cuttings dry out or rot. A viable planting is taken as a couple of kilograms of cuttings. Estimates, not checked against a source.

pyrethrum_stock_kg.basis: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, pyrethrum planting stock (crowns and seed). The perennial is propagated by dividing crowns; the same modest 0.3 increase and 0.1 loss as hop_rhizome_kg, with a viable planting of a couple of kilograms. Estimates, not checked against a source.

dairy_cattle_kg.source: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems' (chapter 5 of the FAO review of ruminant production in sub-Saharan Africa; fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm; undated, 1990s): calving rate 58.7 percent, calf mortality 21.7 percent, adult cow mortality 6.3 percent, age at first calving about 48 months, milk offtake about 250 kg per lactation.
dairy_cattle_kg.basis: Live weight of milk cattle. Half a herd is breeding cows, calving 0.587 a year, and 21.7 percent of calves die, so 0.5 x 0.587 x (1 - 0.217) per head. Loss is the sourced adult mortality. The first calf comes after about four years, so the rate is a steady-state herd figure and a freshly founded herd breeds slower (not modelled). Yield: about 250 kg of milk offtake per cow per lactation in the same systems. The breeding minimum, a bull and three cows, is a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC; the animal weight behind it is not sourced.

pepper_vine_stock_kg.source: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Agritech Portal, 'Horticulture: Spice Crops: Pepper' (agritech.tnau.ac.in/horticulture/horti_spice crops_pepper.html; undated): about 60 cuttings per mother vine per year by the serpentine method, 80 to 85 percent rooting by the trench method, first bearing in the third or fourth year, 2 to 3 kg of dry pepper per vine per year.
pepper_vine_stock_kg.basis: Kilograms of rooted vine cuttings and young vines. Sourced ceiling: 60 cuttings per mother vine at 80 percent rooting, so tens of rooted vines per mother a year; loss is the failed set share, 1 - 0.8. The increase is still capped at a doubling a year, a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, although the yearly growth is now held by the stock's arable land and its labour is bought (sim/engine/living_stock_growth.py): the sourced propagation figures are counts of cuttings or seeds per plant, and no source was found for what a cutting weighs against its mother plant, so a count cannot be turned into a ratio of kilograms; the cap stands for that mass ratio until one is sourced. Years to first yield: three to four. Yield per vine: 2 to 3 kg of dry pepper. A viable planting of a few kilograms is a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC.

tea_plant_stock_kg.source: Clonal propagation of tea (Krishi Vigyan Kendra Mokokchung leaflet; kvkmokokchung.in; undated, as summarised by search): 50 to 300 healthy cuttings per mother bush per year; University of Hawaii CTAHR, 'In-Tray Procedure for Rooting Tea Cuttings' (SCM-35): cutting survival 97 percent in one year and 86 percent in another; tea-industry yield classes of 2000 to 4000 kg of made tea per hectare.
tea_plant_stock_kg.basis: Kilograms of rooted tea cuttings. Sourced ceiling: 50 to 300 cuttings per mother bush a year; loss is the failed share, about 1 - 0.9 from the 86 to 97 percent survival. The increase is still capped at a doubling a year, a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, although the yearly growth is now held by the stock's arable land and its labour is bought (sim/engine/living_stock_growth.py): the sourced propagation figures are counts of cuttings or seeds per plant, and no source was found for what a cutting weighs against its mother plant, so a count cannot be turned into a ratio of kilograms; the cap stands for that mass ratio until one is sourced. Mother bushes are usable after five to six years; first plucking about three to four years after planting out. Yield: 2000 to 4000 kg of made tea per hectare in established fields. The tea-industry yield classes are from a web summary and were not checked in the primary text.

coffee_seedling_kg.source: Agriculture Institute, 'Coffee Propagation Methods: Seed and Vegetative Techniques' (agriculture.institute; undated): nursery loss of 20 to 30 percent to damping-off, temperature and moisture, 6 to 9 months in the nursery, first yield 3 to 4 years from seed; smallholder green-bean yields of 500 to 1000 kg per hectare per year (a coffee-sustainability review, Expl Agric 2005, vol 41, pp 449-473, as summarised by search).
coffee_seedling_kg.basis: Kilograms of coffee seedlings. Loss is the midpoint of the 20 to 30 percent nursery loss, rounded up for field setting. Coffee is raised from seed, a tree bears many seeds, so the propagation ceiling is far above a doubling. The increase is still capped at a doubling a year, a TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, although the yearly growth is now held by the stock's arable land and its labour is bought (sim/engine/living_stock_growth.py): the sourced propagation figures are counts of cuttings or seeds per plant, and no source was found for what a cutting weighs against its mother plant, so a count cannot be turned into a ratio of kilograms; the cap stands for that mass ratio until one is sourced. Years to first yield: three to four. Yield: about 2 to 4 kg of cherry per mature tree, 400 to 800 g of green coffee. Web-summary sources, not handbooks; grade C.

sugar_cane_sett_kg.source: Cane Advisory Services (caneadvisory.ac.in, 'Seed Rate'; undated): 42,000 to 45,000 three-bud setts, 50 to 60 quintals, plant a hectare; a sugarcane planting-techniques review reports a conventional multiplication of about 11 to 12 against 100 to 150 from tissue culture; two-bud setts germinate about 65 to 70 percent (sugarcane agronomy lab manual, mcconline.org.in).
sugar_cane_sett_kg.basis: Kilograms of seed cane (setts). Sourced multiplication: a seed nursery hectare plants about 11 to 12 hectares by conventional multiplication, the same planting rate per hectare in each, so a lot of setts multiplies about eleven-fold in a year (an increase of 10); loss is the failed share, 1 - 0.7 from germination of about 65 to 70 percent. The increase is not capped: the yearly growth is held by the arable land of the stock's place at the nursery output per hectare of the production entry, and its labour is bought at the going wage (sim/engine/living_stock_growth.py). Seed cane per hectare planted: 5000 to 6000 kg. Years to first yield: about one year (a plant cane crop). A planting is not a source of seed after the ratoon crop, which carries disease.

rubber_planting_stock_kg.source: Warren Dean, 'Brazil and the Struggle for Rubber' (Cambridge University Press, 1987) for the 1876 transfer of Hevea seed from the Amazon to Kew and then to Ceylon and Singapore; Sethuraj and Mathew (eds), 'Natural Rubber: Biology, Cultivation and Technology' (Elsevier, 1992) for nursery, budding and tapping practice. Both are named from memory and were not opened in this session; no figure below was checked against their text.
rubber_planting_stock_kg.basis: Kilograms of budded stumps and seedlings of the rubber tree. TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced figures: a budded-stump nursery is taken to double its stock a year (a budwood garden of selected clones gives buds for several stumps each, but what a stump weighs against its mother tree is not known to me, so the doubling stands for that ratio until it is sourced), and about a fifth of stumps are lost in lifting, transport and the first season in the field. A viable planting is taken as a few kilograms. The yearly gain is held by the arable land of the stock's place and its labour is bought (sim/engine/living_stock_growth.py). Years to first tapping: about six to seven for a stump planted out (docs/knowledge/76_farming_food_deep.md, ag2_rubber_plantation, confidence C).

potato_seed_tuber_kg.basis: Seed tubers of the potato. A tuber multiplies only by being planted and lifted, which is the production entry, not a rate of the held lot. SOURCED (read): an Andean organic plot sowed about 1850 kg of seed per hectare and lifted 7.34 kg per kg sown (Quispe Condori and Pari Choquechambi 2025, doi 10.25127/agrops.20252.1087, pp. 6-9; one experimental plot). TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced: half of a held lot lost in a year, since a stored tuber sprouts, rots or shrivels within a season or two without cool dark storage.

maize_seed_kg.basis: Maize grain kept for sowing. Seed multiplies only by being sown and harvested, which is the production entry, not a rate of the held lot. SOURCED (read): milpa sowing is two to three seeds per hill, hills 80 by 40 cm, about 62500 plants per hectare (Cuanalo-de la Cerda and Uicab-Covoh 2006, Terra Latinoamericana 24(3):401-408, p. 404); the seed mass per hectare is not stated. TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced: about a fifth of a held lot unusable after a year, since dry grain keeps viability a few years if kept dry and free of weevil.

cacao_seed_kg.basis: Cacao beans kept for planting. Multiplication is by planting and a bearing tree, which is the production entry, not a rate of the held lot. SOURCED (read): trees become productive two to four years after planting (Daymond et al., Global Review of Cocoa Farming Systems, University of Reading for ICCO, section 2.4). TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, unsourced: nearly all of a held lot lost within a year, since the seed is recalcitrant, does not survive drying and loses viability within weeks unless planted out in a nursery; no source opened for the loss rate.

sheep_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, by the species row. Fresh excreta as a share of live weight a day: USDA NRCS, Agricultural Waste Management Field Handbook, Part 651, chapter 4 'Agricultural Waste Characteristics' (rev. July 1996; opened as a PDF): Table 4-18, lamb waste as excreted, weight 40.00 lb/d/1000#, so 0.04 for sheep; Table 4-8, beef waste as excreted, cow 63.00 lb/d/1000# (feeder yearlings 51.20 to 59.10), so 0.063 for cattle. The chapter has no goat row: goats use the sheep figure (no source found for goats; TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Collected share is the part of the day in a fold, byre or night corral, a third (assumed): dung dropped at pasture is not gathered. Winter ration: dry matter intake of two percent of live weight a day (South Australian government fact sheet 'Calculating dry matter intakes for various classes of stock', Managing livestock in dry times, opened as a PDF: 'Animal on dry pasture or poor quality feed: 2%'; 'Cattle and sheep generally consume between 2-3% of their live weight in DM daily') over ninety days of stall or fold feeding (assumed), half of it straw at ninety percent dry matter (assumed). Bran is a supplement for milked animals (assumed). Confidence D: the excreta share and the dry matter intake are read (above); the collected share, winter days and straw share are assumed.
sheep_kg.source: McKinnon and Rocha, 'Reproduction, mortality and growth of indigenous sheep and goats in Mozambique' (FAO, fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b0w.htm; opened): 79.1 percent of ewes and 91.9 percent of does gave birth in a year, deaths from birth to eight months about 20 percent, whole-flock mortality 16 and 15 percent; litter 1.03 lambs per lambing in an Ethiopian smallholder study (as summarised by a search, not opened). Offtake 20.8 percent a year for sheep (mean of reported traditional-system rates) and mature live weight 28.7 kg ewes, 31.2 kg rams: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems', fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm, opened. Dressing percentage: Montana State University Extension (Sanders County), 'Dressing percentage' note, montana.edu/extension/sanders/understanding%20the%20dressing%20percenage.pdf, opened as a PDF: 'For lambs, the normal range is 44 to 56% with an average of 54 for shorn lambs and 52 for unshorn lambs. For calculations, 50% is often used.' The rest (live weight, fleece, fat and hide shares, salt lick, stocking rate): no source found; kept as labelled heuristics (Complaints/646).
sheep_kg.basis: Live weight of sheep of an unimproved breed, in kilograms. Increase = 0.6 of the flock ewes (assumed) x 0.791 lambing x 1.03 lambs x 0.8 surviving to eight months = 0.391. Loss 0.08 of the flock is adult mortality (assumed: about half the whole-flock mortality sourced above). A breeding group is five animals of about 35 kg, 175 kg (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Herd parameters beside it feed the herd recipe in data/production/95_herds.json: 1.5 head per hectare of rough Mediterranean grazing (the stocking rate the earlier wool entry used, an estimate), a 30 kg mean live weight at slaughter (lambs and culls mixed), a clip of 1 kg greasy wool a head (unimproved breeds; no source found), mutton fat trimmed for rendering 8 percent of the carcass, a raw skin 8 percent of live weight, 4 kg of salt a head-year (about 10 g a day; no source found). Offtake 0.208 is below natural increase less loss (0.31), so the herd is sustained.

goat_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, by the species row. Fresh excreta as a share of live weight a day: USDA NRCS, Agricultural Waste Management Field Handbook, Part 651, chapter 4 'Agricultural Waste Characteristics' (rev. July 1996; opened as a PDF): Table 4-18, lamb waste as excreted, weight 40.00 lb/d/1000#, so 0.04 for sheep; Table 4-8, beef waste as excreted, cow 63.00 lb/d/1000# (feeder yearlings 51.20 to 59.10), so 0.063 for cattle. The chapter has no goat row: goats use the sheep figure (no source found for goats; TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Collected share is the part of the day in a fold, byre or night corral, a third (assumed): dung dropped at pasture is not gathered. Winter ration: dry matter intake of two percent of live weight a day (South Australian government fact sheet 'Calculating dry matter intakes for various classes of stock', Managing livestock in dry times, opened as a PDF: 'Animal on dry pasture or poor quality feed: 2%'; 'Cattle and sheep generally consume between 2-3% of their live weight in DM daily') over ninety days of stall or fold feeding (assumed), half of it straw at ninety percent dry matter (assumed). Bran is a supplement for milked animals (assumed). Confidence D: the excreta share and the dry matter intake are read (above); the collected share, winter days and straw share are assumed.
goat_kg.source: McKinnon and Rocha, 'Reproduction, mortality and growth of indigenous sheep and goats in Mozambique' (FAO, fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b0w.htm; opened): 79.1 percent of ewes and 91.9 percent of does gave birth in a year, deaths from birth to eight months about 20 percent, whole-flock mortality 16 and 15 percent; offtake 21.4 percent a year for goats (mean of reported traditional-system rates) and mature live weight 27.8 kg does, 32.0 kg bucks: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems', fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm, opened. Dressing percentage: Montana State University Extension (Sanders County), 'Dressing percentage' note, opened as a PDF: 'For goats, dressing percentage varies from 40% in very young animals to 56% in entire mature males. 45% is a good average to use.' Okello, 'A survey of the productivity and functions of goats in Uganda', fao.org/4/x5464b/x5464b16.htm, opened, Tables 1-3: dressed carcass weight of Small East African, Mubende and Kigezi goats runs 44.1 to 58.3 percent by sex, age and region, so 45 is at the low end of that survey (kept, the extension average). The rest (litter, live weight, milk per lactation, horn, salt lick, stocking rate) : no source found; kept as labelled heuristics (Complaints/646).
goat_kg.basis: Live weight of goats of an unimproved breed. Increase = 0.6 of the herd does (assumed) x 0.919 kidding x 1.1 kids (assumed) x 0.8 surviving to eight months = 0.485. Loss 0.08 adult mortality (assumed). Breeding group a buck and four does of about 25 kg, 125 kg (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Herd parameters for data/production/95_herds.json: 2 head per hectare of browse (no source found), 25 kg mean live weight at slaughter, half the herd milked for 100 kg a lactation of marketable milk (no source found; 50 kg a head-year), fat 5 percent of a lean carcass, skin 8 percent of live weight, 0.1 kg of horn sheath a head, 3 kg of salt a head-year. Offtake 0.214 is below natural increase less loss (0.405).

cattle_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, by the species row. Fresh excreta as a share of live weight a day: USDA NRCS, Agricultural Waste Management Field Handbook, Part 651, chapter 4 'Agricultural Waste Characteristics' (rev. July 1996; opened as a PDF): Table 4-18, lamb waste as excreted, weight 40.00 lb/d/1000#, so 0.04 for sheep; Table 4-8, beef waste as excreted, cow 63.00 lb/d/1000# (feeder yearlings 51.20 to 59.10), so 0.063 for cattle. The chapter has no goat row: goats use the sheep figure (no source found for goats; TEMPORARY HEURISTIC). Collected share is the part of the day in a fold, byre or night corral, a third (assumed): dung dropped at pasture is not gathered. Winter ration: dry matter intake of two percent of live weight a day (South Australian government fact sheet 'Calculating dry matter intakes for various classes of stock', Managing livestock in dry times, opened as a PDF: 'Animal on dry pasture or poor quality feed: 2%'; 'Cattle and sheep generally consume between 2-3% of their live weight in DM daily') over ninety days of stall or fold feeding (assumed), half of it straw at ninety percent dry matter (assumed). Bran is a supplement for milked animals (assumed). Confidence D: the excreta share and the dry matter intake are read (above); the collected share, winter days and straw share are assumed.
cattle_kg.source: FAO, 'Production parameters of ruminants in traditional systems' (chapter 5 of the FAO review of ruminant production in sub-Saharan Africa; fao.org/4/Y4176E/y4176e08.htm; undated, 1990s), the same source as dairy_cattle_kg: calving rate 58.7 percent, calf mortality 21.7 percent, adult cow mortality 6.3 percent, milk offtake about 250 kg per lactation (opened and quoted: 'The mean of reported offtake rates for cattle in traditional systems is 9.9 percent (median of 9 percent)'; 'The mean weight of mature cows in traditional systems is 244 kg (median of 250 kg)'; 'Milk offtake per lactation in traditional systems is generally low, at an average of 252 kg (median of 251 kg)'). Dressing (45 to 50 percent for zebu-type cattle), fat, hide and horn shares, salt lick (about 30 g a day) and stocking rate: no source found (the chapter does not give them); kept as labelled heuristics (Complaints/670). Draught share of offtake (the share of each year's offtake kept out of the slaughter, castrated and reared to work age at the same live weight): no source found; a labelled heuristic (retire: Complaints/670). A working ox lasts about five years in work (data/world/service_lives.json, Langdon via Medievalists.net).
cattle_kg.basis: Live weight of unselected cattle, in kilograms. Rates are dairy_cattle_kg's (half the herd breeding cows x 0.587 calving x (1 - 0.217) calf survival; adult loss 0.063). Milk per head-year is half the herd x 0.587 calvings x 250 kg a lactation = 73.375 kg. Herd parameters for data/production/95_herds.json: 0.5 head per hectare of extensive grazing, 250 kg live weight at slaughter, dressing 0.48, rendered fat 6 percent of the carcass, green hide 7 percent of live weight, 0.5 kg of horn sheaths a slaughtered animal, 11 kg of salt a head-year. Offtake 0.10 is below natural increase less loss (0.167). Oxen come out of the same herd: draught_share_of_offtake of the year's offtake is kept to work (Complaints/532); mules and horses are still draught_animal_kg's own recipe.

turkey_kg.source: Wikipedia, Wild turkey (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_turkey, opened): 'An adult male (tom or gobbler) normally weighs from 5 to 11 kg', 'the average weight of adult males is 7.6 kg', 'The adult female (hen) is typically much smaller at 2.5-5.4 kg', 'the average weight of adult females is 4.26 kg', 'Hens lay a clutch of 10-14 eggs, usually one per day'. Speller et al. 2018, Diversity of management strategies in Mesoamerican turkeys (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5792941/, opened): in the Postclassic 'turkeys were relying ever more heavily on provisioned maize or other C4 plants', and 'the number of turkey bones in archaeological sites overtakes those of leporids, dogs or white-tailed deer' in the Middle/Late Postclassic (1250-1521 CE). It gives no body weight, egg, flock or offtake figure. Nothing else was read; LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found for the increase and loss rates, the breeding group, dressing percentage, fat and feather shares, maize ration and keeper ratio.
turkey_kg.basis: Live weight of the domestic turkey, kilograms. 5.93 kg is the mean of the opened wild-turkey averages for a tom (7.6 kg) and a hen (4.26 kg), an even sex ratio at slaughter assumed (the Mesoamerican domestic bird's own weight was not found). Increase 1.6 a head: a hen lays one clutch of 12 (middle of the opened 10-14), half the flock are hens, and about a third of eggs reach slaughter age, which is 2 young a bird before losses; 1.6 allows for that being optimistic. TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/654 follow-up (a zooarchaeological flock reconstruction). Loss 0.15 and a breeding group of 18 birds (about one tom to five hens, 5.93 kg each is 107 kg, rounded) are estimates of the same kind. Offtake 1.0 a head-year is below increase less loss (1.45). The birds are fed maize (opened: Postclassic isotopes show provisioned maize), 25 kg a head-year, no source found for the quantity. No pasture: a yard bird, so no land entry and no grows_on.

dog_kg.source: A museum note (https://www.monah.org/artifact-blog/2020/8/21/colima-dogs, opened) cites Sahagun, Florentine Codex 9:48 (Sahagun 1950-1982; the Codex itself not opened): dogs were 'bought ... to provide the people as food'. The note gives no weight, litter or offtake figure. No Mesoamerican dog body mass was found (a search summary gave only a Pathe-site dog about 40.5 cm high, a height, not a weight, and not opened). Nothing else was read; LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found for live weight, increase, loss, breeding group, dressing, fat and hide shares, ration and keeper ratio.
dog_kg.basis: Live weight of the small Mesoamerican dog, 10 kg: TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/654 follow-up (a zooarchaeological body-mass estimate), no source found. Increase 1.2 and loss 0.15 a head are estimates of the same kind (a bitch rearing a couple of pups a year, half the pack bitches); offtake 0.5 is below increase less loss (1.05). A breeding group of 30 kg is three animals. Fed household maize scraps, 60 kg a head-year (no source found). No pasture: a household animal.

pig_kg.dung_and_fodder_source: Dung and fodder per head, as the sheep row (sheep_kg 'dung_and_fodder_source' in this file); no swine row was opened in the NRCS handbook, so the sheep excreta share is borrowed (TEMPORARY HEURISTIC, retire: Complaints/670). Bran: pigs are fed grain offal as well as forage; 60 kg a head-year is an assumed ration (no source found).
pig_kg.source: Varro, De re rustica 2.4 (LacusCurtius, opened through a page fetch, first 100000 characters): the sow 'bears twice a year' (2.4.14), a sow 'can feed eight little pigs at first' (2.4.19), young stay with the dam about two months (2.4.13), a barrow is cut at six months to a year (2.4.21), 'ten boars are enough for 100 sows' (2.4.22). Oyieng, Marshall and Gauly, 'Production parameters estimates of smallholder pig production systems in Uganda' (Tropentag 2023 abstract, https://www.tropentag.de/2023/abstracts/links/Oyieng_Vhqfvk7g.php, opened): litter size 7.2, piglets weaned per sow per year 7.1, farrowing interval 261 days (a modern Ugandan smallholder survey, not a Roman figure). Live weight, dressing, lard share, hide share, stocking rate, salt lick, breeding-sow share, mortality, grain ration and dung: no source found; labelled heuristics (retire: Complaints/670).
pig_kg.basis: Live weight of unimproved pigs, in kilograms. Increase = 0.15 of the herd breeding sows (assumed; Varro's ten boars to 100 sows only fixes the boars) x 7.1 weaned piglets a sow-year (Uganda smallholder survey above) = 1.065 head a head-year.
